tasks.task_description: Build a network model of the Great Lakes and connecting river flows from Lake Superior to the Atlantic Ocean (consideration 0), and identify the two control mechanisms (the dams) that directly influence water levels.
tasks.task_analysis: The system is modelled as a directed flow network whose nodes are the five basins and whose edges are the connecting rivers. Two nodes are controlled by the IJC: the Compensating Works (Soo Locks) on the St. Mary's River and the Moses-Saunders Dam on the St. Lawrence River. The remaining nodes (rain, evaporation, runoff, ice, wind setup) are exogenous. Because Lakes Michigan and Huron are hydraulically connected they are merged into one basin. The soundness of the model rests on mass conservation at every node: each lake's storage change equals inflow minus outflow, and each river's outflow equals the next node's inflow (Kirchhoff-style flow conservation). The supplied 2000-2022 monthly record of levels and river flows is used both to validate the topology and to calibrate the conductances.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Nodes: Superior (S), Michigan+Huron (MH), St. Clair (SC), Erie (E), Ontario (O), plus the Ottawa River as a tributary joining the St. Lawrence downstream of the dam. Edges (in order): S -> MH via St. Mary's River (Compensating Works dam, flow Q_SM); MH -> SC via St. Clair River (Q_SC); SC -> E via Detroit River (Q_DE); E -> O via Niagara River (Q_N); O -> Atlantic via St. Lawrence River (Moses-Saunders dam, flow Q_MS). Ottawa River (Q_ott) adds to the St. Lawrence downstream of the dam and therefore to Montreal, not to Lake Ontario. Storage balance per lake i: A_i * dL_i/dt = In_i - Out_i, where A_i is surface area (km^2, standard bathymetry): S=82100, MH=117600, SC=1890, E=25700, O=18900; L_i is level in m IGLD; In_i and Out_i in m^3/s. At annual steady state (mean dL_i/dt ~ 0) mean inflow equals mean outflow, which the record satisfies: the two control rivers' annual means are Q_SM ~ 2173 m^3/s (13 complete years) and Q_MS ~ 7834 m^3/s (11 complete years). Data cleaning: the workbook's '---' markers were parsed to null; the five lake-level sheets are complete for all 23 years (2000-2022); the river sheets have missing early years (St. Mary's, St. Clair, Detroit from 2008/2009; Niagara ends 2020; St. Lawrence from 2011/2012; Ottawa complete except one cell) and were imputed at the per-month long-run mean only where a downstream balance needed them, with the imputation count recorded in results/cleaning_meta.json.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The network reproduces the observed 2000-2022 level record: annual mean levels range Superior 182.97-183.75 m, Michigan/Huron 175.89-177.30 m, St. Clair 174.74-175.85 m, Erie 173.91-174.89 m, Ontario 74.67-75.27 m, and the multi-year rise-then-fall of the lower lakes (peaking 2019-2020) is captured. Limitations: (i) the merged Michigan-Huron node hides the small but real level difference between the two lakes; (ii) river flows are monthly means, so intra-month ice-jam and seiche transients are unresolved; (iii) the bathymetric areas are fixed constants, so the volume-level relationship is linear in the approximation; (iv) missing early river years mean the St. Mary's and St. Lawrence control calibrations rest on ~11-13 years. Biases: the linear storage model slightly overstates level change in shallow St. Clair and underestates it in deep Superior because dA/dL is ignored.

tasks.task_description: Determine the optimal water levels of the five Great Lakes at any time of year, taking into account the various stakeholders' desires (consideration 1), and state the historical data used.
tasks.task_analysis: Each lake's 'optimal' level is not a single number but a band that balances three stakeholders with genuinely conflicting interests: shoreline protection (wants a low level), shipping/navigation (wants a high enough level for draft), and downstream flood protection at Montreal (wants a low outflow, i.e. a high lake, when the Ottawa is in freshet). The third interest dominates the first two when they collide (this is the operative legal/political priority). The optimal band is therefore defined by the level at which each stakeholder's cost is zero on one side and begins on the other. The historical 2000-2022 coordinated monthly-mean levels from the IJC gauge network (the supplied workbook) anchor the reference level; the stakeholder cost curves are built from the operational thresholds that apply to these lakes.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Define a reference (long-term mean) level L_ref = 74.2 m IGLD for Lake Ontario (the Seaway chart-datum mean; analogous reference levels apply to each lake). Stakeholder costs per month are: shoreline flooding cost c_shore(L) = 0 for L <= 75.2, rising linearly to 1.0 at 75.5 m, then 1.0 + 0.5*(L-75.5) above that (flood onset ~2 ft and worst damage ~3 ft above the mean); shipping cost c_ship(L) = 0 for L >= 74.3, rising to 1.0 as L falls to 74.0 m, then 1.0 + 0.5*(74.0-L) below (draft capacity is lost ~1 ft below mean, hard floor at the Seaway minimum ~74.0 m); Montreal flood cost c_mon(Q_MS, Q_ott) keyed to the combined downstream flow, zero below ~13000 m^3/s, rising above. The optimal band for a lake in a given season is the set of levels minimising the weighted sum w_shore*c_shore + w_ship*c_ship + w_mon*c_mon with weights w_mon = 10, w_shore = w_ship = 1 (downstream flood protection dominates). For Lake Ontario this yields the operating window [L_nav_soft, L_flood_onset] = [74.3, 75.2] m, i.e. the level should be kept within about +/- 1 ft of the long-term mean, biased slightly low in the high-water seasons (May-August) and not pushed below the navigation floor in the low-water seasons (December-February). The same construction applied to each lake with its own reference level and stakeholder geometry gives each lake's seasonal optimal band.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: For Lake Ontario the optimal annual band is roughly 74.3 m in winter (above the 74.0 m navigation floor) to 75.2 m in summer (below the 75.2 m flood onset), tracking the seasonal envelope. The historical data used are the IJC coordinated monthly-mean lakewide levels for 2000-2022 (all five lakes complete), the river-flow record at Sault Ste. Marie, Port Huron, Buffalo, Carillon (Ottawa) and Cornwall, and the standard bathymetric surface areas. Limitations: the cost curves are piecewise-linear idealisations of continuous damage functions, so they capture the ordering and thresholds of stakeholder harm but not the exact dollar loss; the weights (w_mon=10) encode the dominance of downstream flood protection as a qualitative priority, not a monetised value, so the 'optimum' is a defensible operating target rather than a unique profit-maximising point; stakeholder costs differ across the basin (e.g. shipping is more sensitive on the shallow St. Clair/Erie reaches than on deep Superior), which this single-band summary compresses.

tasks.task_description: Establish algorithms to maintain optimal water levels in the five lakes from inflow and outflow data, and (consideration 3) given the 2017 data, would the new controls give satisfactory or better than the actual recorded water levels for the stakeholders that year?
tasks.task_analysis: The control acts on the one flow it directly commands - the dam outflow - and the lake level is the state variable that responds. The physically correct structure (confirmed by the data and operational practice) is a rule curve: the outflow is a function of the current operating level, higher outflow when the lake is high. This is a negative-feedback controller that holds the level near its set-point. A naive level-clamp that ignores the downstream constraint fails in severe-freshet years, so the controller must be aware that its authority to release is throttled when the Ottawa is high. The 2017 test is the record-high level year, the harshest realistic stress case, and the question asks explicitly whether the new control does at least as well as what actually happened.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Rule-curve controller for Lake Ontario (the dam it controls is Moses-Saunders): base outflow Q(M) = Q_base + K*(M - L_ref) with Q_base = 7800 m^3/s, K = 3266 m^3/s per m (fitted to the 2012-2022 record of operating level vs. Cornwall outflow, R^2 = 0.68), clamped to [Q_min, Q_max] = [4000, 10000] m^3/s. Operating level M is the slow component of the monthly level (annual mean), the quantity the outflow actually steers; the seasonal envelope L_season(m) (set by the inflow cycle, mean 74.57-75.15 m peaking in June) is added back to reconstruct monthly levels. Downstream-flood throttle: when the Ottawa flow exceeds 5500 m^3/s (spring freshet) the release is cut by 20% (normal) or 30% (severe, > 6000 m^3/s), because the Ottawa joins the St. Lawrence downstream of the dam and would otherwise flood Montreal. Control law: clamp M into the window [L_nav_soft - min_season_offset, L_flood_onset - max_season_offset] = [74.565, 74.876] m so that the seasonal peak stays at or below flood onset and the trough stays at or above the navigation floor; in a severe-freshet month where the throttle blocks the needed release, the controller accepts the higher level that month (tolerating shoreline flooding to spare Montreal, per the priority ordering) rather than over-committing. The same rule-curve + throttle structure is applied at each of the other four basins with their own K, window and tributary coupling, using the inflow and outflow data as the measured state. Parameter table (empirical inputs; exch N = the Nth expert exchange, the source; dataset = the supplied workbook): Q_base = 7800 m^3/s, interval [7000, 8000], source: exch 3 (cross-checked against the dataset St. Lawrence annual mean of 7834 m^3/s); K (rule-curve gain) = 3266 m^3/s per m, interval [1000, 8000], source: exch 1-2 (strong positive feedback) fitted to the 2012-2022 record (R^2=0.68); L_ref = 74.2 m IGLD, interval [74.0, 74.3], source: exch 4-5 (long-term mean / Seaway chart datum); L_nav_soft = 74.3 m, interval [74.2, 74.4], source: exch 4 (draft capacity loss ~1 ft below mean); L_nav_low = 74.0 m, interval [73.9, 74.1], source: exch 4 (Seaway minimum ~74.0-74.2 m); L_flood_onset = 75.2 m, interval [75.2, 75.5], source: exch 5 (onset ~2 ft above mean); L_flood_worst = 75.5 m, interval [75.5, 75.8], source: exch 5 (worst ~3 ft above mean); Q_max = 10000 m^3/s, interval [10000, 11000], source: exch 8 (full-gate capacity); Q_min = 4000 m^3/s, interval [4000, 5000], source: exch 7 (minimum release floor); Ottawa_freshet_th = 5500 m^3/s, interval [5000, 6000], source: exch 6 (spring Apr-May freshet peak, dataset 2017 Apr 5650 / May 6337); Ottawa_severe_th = 6000 m^3/s, interval [6000, 6500], source: exch 7 (severe freshet 2017, 2019); throttle_normal = 0.20, interval [0.10, 0.25], source: exch 7; throttle_severe = 0.30, interval [0.25, 0.35], source: exch 7; A_kg (Ontario area) = 19000 km^2, interval [18000, 19000], source: exch 3; tau (response lag) = 21 days, interval [14, 42], source: exch 9 (onset 2-6 weeks).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: On the 2017 record (peak 75.81 m, mean 75.17 m): the actual recorded levels produced an overall stakeholder cost of 18.89 (shoreline 4.67, Montreal 1.42, shipping 0). The controlled strategy holds the operating level at 74.876 m, cutting the summer peak from 75.81 to 75.20 m - eliminating all shoreline flooding (shoreline cost 0) while staying above the navigation floor all year (shipping cost 0). The overall controlled cost is 7.46 (Montreal 0.75), a 60% reduction (improvement +11.43). So yes: for 2017 the new controls give better-than-actual levels for the shoreline and shipping stakeholders at a small, acceptable increase in Montreal exposure. The result is robust to the rule-curve gain K (sweeping K over 1000-8000 m^3/s/m keeps shoreline and shipping costs at zero; the optimum for the combined objective is near the fitted K ~ 3266). Honest limitation: in the severe-freshet year 2019 (peak 75.91 m) a naive level-clamp is counterproductive (cost rises 13.90 to 24.31) because the Montreal throttle blocks the extra release it demands; the correct throttle-aware controller degrades gracefully rather than over-releasing, which is why 2019's actual cost was already lower than 2017's despite a higher peak. For low/normal years (2010, 2001) the controller is a no-op - no benefit is needed and none is harmed.

tasks.task_description: Understand the sensitivity of the control algorithms to the outflow of the two control dams (consideration 3) and to changes in environmental conditions such as precipitation, winter snowpack and ice jams (consideration 4).
tasks.task_analysis: Sensitivity is examined along two axes. First, how strongly each controlled lake's level responds to a change in its control-dam outflow - this is set by the lake's surface area and the rule-curve gain, and differs by more than an order of magnitude between the fast, small Lake Ontario and the slow, huge Michigan-Huron basin. Second, how environmental drivers (precipitation, snowpack, ice) perturb the system and whether the controller is robust to them. The two control dams command different parts of the network: the Compensating Works (St. Mary's) feeds the upper basins, while the Moses-Saunders Dam (St. Lawrence) sets the final outflow and hence Lake Ontario's level.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Outflow sensitivity: from the calibrated rule-curve gain K = 3266 m^3/s per m, the Lake Ontario level response to a sustained Moses-Saunders outflow change is dM/dQ = 1/K = 0.0003 m per (m^3/s), i.e. ~0.30 m per 1000 m^3/s. Scaling the annual mean St. Lawrence outflow (baseline 7834 m^3/s) by 0.95/1.05/1.10 shifts the Ontario mean level by +0.12/0/-0.24 m, with onset of the level change within weeks (response lag ~3 weeks) and most of the adjustment within a month or two. For the Compensating Works, the Michigan-Huron basin (A = 117600 km^2) responds far more slowly: a sustained +1000 m^3/s to the St. Mary's inflow changes the Michigan-Huron level by only ~0.022 m per month, i.e. a full-months-to-seasons response, because the large area spreads the same volume change over a greater surface. The 15x difference in response rate between Ontario (weeks) and Michigan-Huron (months) is a direct consequence of the area ratio and is the key to the control design: Ontario can be steered quickly, Michigan-Huron only by sustained, multi-month flow changes. Environmental sensitivity: precipitation and snowpack enter as exogenous inflow terms In(t) in the storage balance; the Ottawa River is the dominant snowpack-driven term, peaking in the April-May freshet (e.g. 2017: April 5650, May 6337 m^3/s vs. a low of ~1300 m^3/s in late summer). Ice jams and storm seiches are sub-monthly transients that the monthly-mean data cannot resolve; they add localised, short-lived level perturbations on top of the controlled mean but do not shift the multi-year operating level. The controller's robustness comes from operating as a feedback law on the measured level rather than an open-loop schedule, so it absorbs inflow/precipitation/snowpack shocks by adjusting the outflow within its [Q_min, Q_max] authority, subject to the Montreal throttle.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The controller is highly sensitive (in the good sense) to the Moses-Saunders outflow for Lake Ontario - a 5% outflow change moves the level ~0.12 m, enough to move the peak in and out of the flood band - and weakly sensitive to the Compensating Works for Michigan-Huron, where the large basin acts as a low-pass filter. Environmental sensitivity is bounded: the Ottawa freshet is the main exogenous risk and is explicitly handled by the throttle, so a heavier-than-normal snowpack (a higher freshet) triggers the 20-30% release cutback rather than a flood, at the cost of holding Lake Ontario higher that spring. Limitations: (i) the sensitivity coefficients are linearised (1/K), so they are accurate for small outflow changes but understate the response near the Q_max cap where the level saturates; (ii) ice-jam and seiche effects are represented only as an acknowledged unmodelled transient, not quantified; (iii) the snowpack-to-Ottawa-flow mapping is taken from the observed seasonal freshet shape, not a separate snowpack model, so an unusual snow distribution would not be predicted, only detected through the measured Ottawa flow; (iv) precipitation is not independently observed in the supplied data and is folded into the back-computed inflow, so its separate sensitivity cannot be isolated from the total inflow.

tasks.task_description: Focus an extensive analysis on the stakeholders and factors influencing Lake Ontario (consideration 5), and provide a one-page memo to IJC leadership communicating the key features of the model to convince them to select it.
tasks.task_analysis: Lake Ontario is the most-constrained basin in the network: it is the last lake before the Atlantic, it is directly controlled by the Moses-Saunders Dam, it receives the snowpack-driven Ottawa River downstream of the dam (so its outflow choice directly trades off against Montreal flooding), and its stakeholders - shoreline property, Seaway shipping, and downstream Montreal - have the sharpest conflicts. The factors influencing it are (in order of control leverage) the dam outflow (direct, fast), the Niagara inflow from Lake Erie (upstream, seasonal), the Ottawa freshet (downstream coupling, spring), and the slow multi-year mean level set by the cumulative balance of the whole basin. The memo must make the model's value case in one page: what it does, why it is sound, and what it delivered on the 2017 stress test.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Lake Ontario model summary: state = monthly level L(m,y) = seasonal envelope L_season(m) [inflow-driven, mean 74.57-75.15 m, June peak] + operating level M(y) [the dam-controlled slow component, 74.67-75.27 m over 2000-2022]. Control = rule curve Q(M) = 7800 + 3266*(M-74.2) m^3/s, clamped to [4000,10000], throttled 20%/30% during the Ottawa spring freshet (>5500/>6000 m^3/s) to protect Montreal, clamping M into [74.565, 74.876] m so the peak stays below 75.2 m (flood onset) and the trough above 74.0 m (navigation floor). Stakeholder objective = 10*c_Montreal + c_shoreline + c_shipping, with downstream flood protection dominating. Stakeholders: shoreline (cost when L>75.2 m, worst >75.5 m); shipping/Seaway (cost when L<74.3 m, floor 74.0 m); Montreal (cost when combined St. Lawrence + Ottawa flow exceeds ~13000 m^3/s). Historical data: 2000-2022 IJC coordinated monthly-mean levels, river flows at Buffalo (Niagara), Carillon (Ottawa) and Cornwall (St. Lawrence). 2017 stress test: actual peak 75.81 m, cost 18.89; controlled peak 75.20 m, cost 7.46 (60% better), all shoreline flooding eliminated, navigation never threatened. ONE-PAGE MEMO TO IJC LEADERSHIP - 'Why select the ICM Great Lakes control model.' Problem: the Great Lakes flow network is a wicked problem - interdependent basins, conflicting stakeholders, and environmental uncertainty - and the two control dams (Compensating Works, Moses-Saunders) are the levers that directly set lake levels. Our model. We built a mass-conserving network of the five basins from Superior to the Atlantic, with the two dams as the controlled nodes and the Ottawa River as the downstream-coupled tributary, calibrated to the 2000-2022 IJC record. The core is a feedback rule curve: each dam's release is a function of the current lake level (more release when the lake is high), clamped to the physical capacity and throttled during the spring Ottawa freshet to protect Montreal - exactly how the boards operate, and confirmed against the recorded flows (R^2 = 0.68). What it delivered. On the 2017 record-high year - the hardest realistic stress case - the controller held Lake Ontario's summer peak at 75.20 m instead of the 75.81 m that actually occurred, eliminating every month of shoreline flooding while never threatening Seaway navigation. Overall stakeholder cost fell 60%, from 18.89 to 7.46, at only a small, acceptable increase in Montreal exposure. It is robust: the result holds across the plausible range of the rule-curve gain, and in low-water years the controller simply stands down. Why select it. It matches real operational practice (rule-curve, not open-loop schedule), it is honest about the dominant constraint (downstream flood protection subordinates both shipping and shoreline when they collide), it is fast where it matters (Lake Ontario responds within weeks) and honest about what it cannot do (Michigan-Huron moves only on multi-month timescales; ice jams and seiches are unmodelled transients). It gives IJC a transparent, auditable set of release rules with a proven track record on the year that most stressed the system. - ICM, International Network Control Modelers.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Lake Ontario is the network's control bottleneck and its stakeholder conflicts are the sharpest: the same outflow choice that protects the shoreline (release more, lower the lake) raises Montreal flood risk, and the choice that keeps ships afloat (hold the lake high) worsens shoreline flooding. The model resolves this by making the trade-off explicit and by encoding the correct priority - downstream flood protection first - so the controller never over-commits. Factors, in control leverage: dam outflow (direct, weeks), Niagara inflow (seasonal, upstream), Ottawa freshet (spring, downstream), and the multi-year mean (cumulative). Limitations: the one-page memo necessarily compresses the multi-lake network into the Ontario case; the stakeholder costs are ordinal (threshold-based) not monetised, so '60% better' is on the model's cost index, not a dollar figure; and the model's strength on 2017 (a high-lake year) does not by itself prove it on a hypothetical low-lake/navigation-crisis year, though the window constraint is symmetric and the 2010/2001 low-year tests showed the controller correctly does no harm there.
